entries.title: Eye Level
entries.text:
Eye Level

An eye-level shot places the camera at the subject's eye height with a horizontal sightline and a level horizon. It is the default equal relationship: height and tilt assign no rank until you leave this setup.

Create this Eye Level

Narrative function

Rank in a frame comes from where the lens sits and how it is pitched. Eye-level refuses that assignment.

Two people at matching eye height read as peers; the room does not look down on them, and they do not loom. Sit when they sit.

Stand when they stand. The judgment, if any, has to come from performance, costume, or light, not from geometry.

It is the wrong tool when the beat is surveillance, monument, or a map. A few degrees of pitch and you have already cut to a High Angle or a Low Angle.

A few inches down and you are in Shoulder Level, which is a companion, not a peer.

How it works

Match the nodal point to the subject's eyes. Keep roll at zero so verticals stay vertical.

A 35mm to 50mm keeps perspective close to human vision; a wide from the same height will still stretch the room without changing rank. Height and tilt are independent: a camera at eye height that looks down is no longer an eye-level shot, it is a high angle from eye height.

Prompt it as camera at their eye height, horizon level, no tilt up or down.

When to use it

Use it for a conversation that should not take sides, or for a face you want believed without the camera lobbying. Concrete beat: two adults at a kitchen table, seated eyes matched, no ceiling grab.

Do not look down or up unless you mean it.

Compared with similar shots

High Angle pitches down and shrinks the figure. Low Angle pitches up and grows it.

Shoulder Level sits a few inches below the eyes, like a walking companion. Point of View is what the character sees, not a camera beside them at the same height.

Over-the-Shoulder Coverage keeps a near body in the foreground; eye-level can be a clean Single.

High AngleVulnerability, surveillance, or a map of a room.

Low AnglePower, monument, or intimidation.

Bird's-Eye ViewTurn life into a board game or a ritual.

In film

Tokyo Story holds domestic talk at human height so posture, not a power tilt, does the judging. Rosetta stays with her at her own eye line as she moves, refusing a look down.

Use those as grammar: match height to the person in the scene, keep the horizon honest.

Prompt it

Lead with height and pitch. Quote: Eye-level shot of [Subject], camera at their eye height, horizontal sightline, equal relationship, no power tilt.

Name that the horizon is level. Add a 35mm or 50mm if you want human perspective.

Do not write mood words in place of the height.

Use in Image Generator

Eye-level shot of [Subject], camera at their eye height, horizontal sightline, equal relationship, no power tilt.

What usually goes wrong

The usual wrong cousin is a mild Low Angle, because generators treat a portrait as a poster. Tell: ceiling in frame, chin from below, verticals converging.

Fix: camera at eye height, horizon level, no tilt. If the subject is seated, sit the camera; standing eye-level on a seated person is already looking down.

Questions

What is eye level in film?

An eye-level shot places the camera at the subject's eye height with a level horizon. The sightline is horizontal, so the frame does not assign power by looking up or down.

Eye level vs high angle

Eye level matches the subject's eyes and stays level. A high-angle shot raises the camera and pitches it down, so more floor enters and the figure occupies less of the rectangle.

When should I use eye level?

Use it when the relationship should read as equal: talk, witness, default coverage. Skip it when the beat needs vulnerability from above or monument from below.

How do I prompt eye level for AI image or video?

Write: Eye-level shot of [Subject], camera at their eye height, horizon level, no tilt up or down. Name sit versus stand so the model does not look down on a seated body.

entries.title: High Angle
entries.text:
High Angle

High angle shotPlongéeElevated observation

A high-angle shot looks downward at the subject from above eye level, an oblique pitch rather than a straight drop. More floor enters the frame, the figure occupies less of the rectangle, and the viewpoint reads as observation from above.

Volume

Create this High Angle

Narrative function

Height plus downward tilt is what assigns the smaller rank. A high angle can be pity, surveillance, or a clinical map of who can reach the door.

The face should still be a face: you see the crown and the shoulders, not only a scalp. Paths and distances that Eye Level would hide become readable because the floor is a diagram with walls still receding.

It is the wrong tool when you need a true plan view. If the tabletop must be a rectangle and bodies become pieces, you wanted Overhead Top-Down or a steep Bird's-Eye View.

It is also the wrong tool for a power confrontation; looking down on the boss fights the line.

How it works

Raise the camera above the subject's eyes and pitch it down. Typical working range is a step-stool to a short ladder, 20 to 45 degrees of tilt, subject still recognizable through costume and contrast.

Top-light and ceiling practicals become the key more often, because you are now closer to the lights that hang. Keep roll level; a canted high angle is two techniques at once.

Prompt: high-angle shot looking down, figure diminished, more floor than sky, not top-down.

When to use it

Use it for vulnerability, surveillance, or a map of a room that eye-level cannot draw. Concrete beat: a lone figure on a station platform, camera above the lamps, suitcase readable on the boards.

Do not use a high oblique when the shot must be strictly top-down.

Compared with similar shots

Eye Level stays on the sightline and assigns no rank. Bird's-Eye View looks steeply or straight down from a great height until people are a map.

Overhead Top-Down is 90 degrees, a flat-lay or room plan. Low Angle is the opposing pitch.

Crane Over is the move that can arrive at a high or overhead view.

Bird's-Eye ViewTurn life into a board game or a ritual.

Low AnglePower, monument, or intimidation.

Eye LevelDefault honesty. Do not look down or up unless you mean it.

In film

Psycho uses a steep high view on the stairway so Arbogast is placed inside the house's geometry before the attack. The Shawshank Redemption uses high views of the prison so human scale sits inside the walls.

Citizen Kane and Prisoners both look down when a person should feel watched or reduced. Borrow the downward pitch and the readable floor, not a poster.

Psycho 1960The overhead view during Arbogast’s stairway encounter.

The Shawshank Redemption 1994High views establish the prison and its constrained human scale.

Prompt it

Name the look-down, not only camera up high. Quote: High-angle shot looking down on [Subject], the figure diminished, architecture or sky weighing on them.

Add: oblique angle, face still readable, more floor than ceiling, horizon not level to the eyes. Forbid 90-degree top-down unless you actually want Overhead Top-Down.

Use in Video Generator

High oblique view of a lone cleaner crossing a vast empty railway hall after midnight. The architecture and floor pattern dominate. The cleaner pauses at a distant sound. Fixed elevated viewpoint, no drone swoop or zoom.

What usually goes wrong

The usual wrong cousin is Bird's-Eye View or Overhead Top-Down: the model snaps to a drone plan. Tell: tops of heads only, table as a perfect rectangle, no face.

Fix: looking down 30 degrees, eyes and mouth still readable, walls receding. The other failure is a raised camera that stays level, which is a high vantage, not a high angle.

Questions

What is a high angle in film?

A high-angle shot looks down at the subject from above eye level. The pitch is oblique, so you still read a person, only smaller in their space.

High angle vs bird's-eye view

A high angle is a downward look that keeps the face and the room in perspective. A bird's-eye view is much higher and steeper, often nearly straight down, until life reads as a map.

When should I use a high angle?

Use it when someone is vulnerable, watched, or when the floor plan of a room matters more than a power face. Do not use it as a default dramatic portrait.

How do I prompt a high angle for AI image or video?

Write: High-angle shot looking down on [Subject], figure diminished, more floor than ceiling, face still readable, not top-down. Name an approximate tilt if the model keeps flattening the room.

entries.title: Low Angle
entries.text:
Low Angle

Low angle shotTatami-level compositionOzu-style low camera

A low-angle shot looks upward at the subject from below eye level, so verticals converge and ceilings or sky take weight. The camera is not merely low; it is pitched up, and that pitch is what assigns monument or intimidation.

Volume

Create this Low Angle

Narrative function

Looking up makes a body into architecture. Door frames, ceiling beams, and the underside of a chin enter the picture.

A boss in a doorway, a statue, a threat: the subject occupies the top of the frame and we occupy the floor. Citizen Kane built ceilings (and sometimes dug a pit) so the look-up had a real lid.

Do not confuse this with a low camera that stays level. A tatami or seated-height camera with a horizontal sightline is a height choice, close to seated Eye Level, not a low angle.

Ozu's rooms sit low without turning the family into towers. If you pitch up on that setup, you have changed the sentence.

It is the wrong tool for a peer conversation and for a true worm's view of a skyscraper. Moderate look-up is a portrait with rank.

Extreme look-up is Worm's-Eye View.

How it works

Drop the camera below the subject's eyes (chest, waist, or a hole in the floor) and tilt up until verticals converge toward the top of the frame. A wider lens exaggerates the convergence; a longer lens from the same height still looks up but with less stretch.

Practicals on the ceiling become motivated keys. Keep roll level unless you are also doing a Dutch Angle.

Prompt: low-angle looking up, converging verticals, ceiling or sky in frame, not camera on the dirt looking straight up.

When to use it

Use it for power, monument, or intimidation: someone who should fill the doorway. Concrete beat: a standing figure shot from a seated listener, ceiling beams closing over the head.

Do not pitch up on every protagonist as a default poster.

Compared with similar shots

Eye Level keeps the sightline horizontal. Worm's-Eye View looks sharply up from ground or below until the subject is a tower and verticals collapse inward.

Ground Level is a floor-height camera; it may look along the dirt instead of up. High Angle is the opposing pitch.

Trunk Shot looks up from inside a container, which is a location, not only a tilt.

Worm's-Eye ViewThe subject is a tower. You are dust.

High AngleVulnerability, surveillance, or a map of a room.

Eye LevelDefault honesty. Do not look down or up unless you mean it.

In film

Citizen Kane puts ceilings and looming bodies into confrontations by looking up from a lowered camera. Touch of Evil uses the same grammar on Quinlan so bulk becomes the image.

The Dark Knight often pitches up on costume and architecture so the figure reads as a structure. Tokyo Story and Late Spring are the usual mix-up: low seated cameras, mostly level, not this tilt.

Tokyo Story 1953Domestic conversations filmed from a low, stable viewpoint.

Late Spring 1949Seated interiors and carefully arranged domestic exchanges.

Citizen Kane 1941Low-angle confrontations make ceilings and looming bodies part of the image.

Touch of Evil 1958Quinlan’s imposing low-angle appearances.

Prompt it

Name the look-up and the ceiling. Quote: Low-angle shot looking up at [Subject], converging verticals, heroic or oppressive height, Citizen Kane floor.

Add: camera below their eyes, horizon low, ceiling or sky in frame, face still a portrait. Ban from the ground looking straight up unless you want Worm's-Eye View.

Use in Video Generator

A quiet family conversation in a modest room, filmed from a low seated height with the camera level. Two adults sit beside a low table, doorways carefully balanced, no dramatic upward angle. Locked shot, small natural gestures, patient pauses.

What usually goes wrong

The usual wrong cousin is Worm's-Eye View or a generic Ground Level boot shot. Tell: only nostrils and a vanishing point in the sky, or only shoes.

Fix: below eye height, tilted up, eyes and mouth still readable, ceiling in. The other mix-up is Ozu: low height, level camera.

If doorways and floor lines stay orthogonal, you never pitched up.

Questions

What is a low angle in film?

A low-angle shot looks up at the subject from below eye level. Verticals converge, ceilings or sky gain area, and the figure reads larger than an eye-level portrait.

Low angle vs worm's-eye view

A low angle is a moderate look-up that still functions as a face. A worm's-eye view is extreme: lens at or below ground, looking sharply up, verticals collapsing inward, the subject as a tower.

When should I use a low angle?

Use it when power, monument, or intimidation should be in the geometry: a standing threat over a seated listener, a figure in a doorway. Do not use it as default flattery.

How do I prompt a low angle for AI image or video?

Write: Low-angle shot looking up at [Subject], camera below their eyes, converging verticals, ceiling in frame. Say it is not a worm's-eye or floor-only boot shot.

entries.title: Bird's-Eye View
entries.text:
Bird's-Eye View

top downoverhead still

A bird's-eye view shot looks steeply or directly down from a great height so people and furniture become a map. Height, not just distance, is the point of view: life reads as a board game or a ritual seen from above.

Volume

Create this Bird's-Eye View

Narrative function

From up there the body is a token. Circulation, grouping, and the shape of a courtyard or a table take over.

You use it to turn a fight, a dinner, or a street into a pattern the participants cannot see. The camera is high enough that the floor is the picture, but unlike a close Overhead Top-Down you still feel drop: altitude, not a light stand over a desk.

It is the wrong tool when you need a face, a line of dialogue, or a simple sense that someone is small in a room. That last job is often a High Angle from a balcony.

If the model flies and tours, you have left the still viewpoint for a drone move.

How it works

Place the camera well above the action and pitch it steeply down, approaching 70 to 90 degrees. Great height is required: a ceiling corner of a lobby, a crane, a rooftop, a high grid.

Anatomy foreshortens; heads and shoulders become discs. Keep extra limbs out of a seated tableau or the map grows a mutant.

Light from above will flatten; a raking key throws shadows as drawing on the floor. Prompt: bird's-eye straight down from a great height, floor as a map, no extra limbs.

When to use it

Use it to turn life into a board game or a ritual. Concrete beat: one seated person and a table seen from the ceiling so plates and hands are the story.

Do not use it as a sightseeing flyover when the beat is still a person.

Compared with similar shots

High Angle looks down obliquely; the face remains a face. Overhead Top-Down is a 90-degree top-down, often closer, a flat-lay or room plan whose tabletop must stay rectangular.

Crane Over is the path that can arrive at a bird's-eye. Aerial and FPV Drone add flight; bird's-eye can be a locked steep look.

Overhead Top-DownTable, crime scene, or dance formation.

High AngleVulnerability, surveillance, or a map of a room.

Eye LevelDefault honesty. Do not look down or up unless you mean it.

In film

The Grand Budapest Hotel uses steep downward views so hotels, desks, and ceremonies read as designed diagrams. Requiem for a Dream looks down until apartments and bodies are patterns of habit.

Use the altitude and the map, not a copied lobby.

Prompt it

Lock height and pitch. Quote: Bird's-eye view straight down on [Subject], camera over one seated person and a table, floor as a map, no extra limbs.

Add: great height, steeply downward, people as pieces, not an oblique high angle, not a tabletop product flat-lay unless the scale is a room seen from the ceiling.

Use in Image Generator

Bird's-eye view straight down on [Subject], camera over one seated person and a table, floor as a map, no extra limbs.

What usually goes wrong

The usual wrong cousin is a mild High Angle (too little height) or a close Overhead Top-Down (too little altitude, too much product photography). Tell: a readable standing portrait from a step-stool, or a desk filling the frame with no drop.

Fix: camera high above, looking steeply down, bodies foreshortened, floor as geography. Ban extra arms in seated groups.

Questions

What is bird's-eye view in film?

A bird's-eye view looks steeply or straight down from a great height. People and furniture become a map; altitude is the viewpoint.

Bird's-eye view vs overhead

Bird's-eye implies great height and a map of a place. Overhead top-down is 90 degrees and often closer: a table, a crime scene, or a dance as a graphic plan.

When should I use bird's-eye view?

Use it when grouping, ritual, or circulation should win over any one face. Do not use it for dialogue or for a product lying on a table.

How do I prompt bird's-eye view for AI image or video?

Write: Bird's-eye view straight down on [Subject] from a great height, floor as a map, bodies foreshortened, no extra limbs. Say not a high-angle portrait and not a 90-degree desk flat-lay.

entries.title: Worm's-Eye View
entries.text:
Worm's-Eye View

A worm's-eye view looks sharply upward from ground level or below the subject, an extreme low pitch that collapses verticals inward. The subject is a tower and the camera is dust.

Create this Worm's-Eye View

Narrative function

This is not a slightly taller portrait. The lens is on or under the floor plane and the look is nearly straight up: nostrils, cornices, the belly of a ship, a ceiling that has become the whole sky.

Wonder and terror share the same geometry because scale has nowhere to go but over you. Use a Low Angle when you still need a face that can speak.

Use Ground Level when the dirt, the boots, and the trailing hem are the actors and the look may travel along the ground rather than up the body. Worm's-eye is the vanishing point in the zenith.

How it works

Put the lens on the floor, in a pit, or at ground grade. Tilt up hard, often past 60 degrees, until architecture converges to a point above the frame.

Ultra-wide glass increases the collapse; keep anatomy plausible (one head, two feet). Foreground may include earth, a curb, or a grating.

Prompt: worm's-eye from ground level looking straight up, extreme low, verticals collapsing inward.

When to use it

Use it when the subject should erase you: a spacecraft hull, a courthouse, a giant. Concrete beat: looking straight up the wall of a ship or a tower so the person is architecture.

Do not use it for a simple power two-shot; that is a Low Angle.

Compared with similar shots

Low Angle looks up from below the eyes and still delivers a portrait. Ground Level names the height of the lens on the floor; it can look along boots instead of straight up.

Trunk Shot looks up from inside a container with a rim. High Angle and Bird's-Eye View are the opposing downward family.

Low AnglePower, monument, or intimidation.

Ground LevelStart from the dirt.

Eye LevelDefault honesty. Do not look down or up unless you mean it.

In film

Citizen Kane pushes some interiors past a working low angle into a pit look, ceilings crushing the figure. Arrival stages the shell so humans look up from grass and become small against a hull.

Borrow the extreme upward pitch and the collapse of verticals.

Prompt it

Say straight up, not merely low. Quote: Worm's-eye view from ground level looking straight up at [Subject], extreme low, verticals collapsing inward, awe or terror.

Add: lens on the dirt or in a pit, architecture towering, face foreshortened from below. Not a waist-height power tilt.

Use in Image Generator

Worm's-eye view from ground level looking straight up at [Subject], extreme low, verticals collapsing inward, awe or terror.

What usually goes wrong

The usual wrong cousin is Low Angle. Tell: a readable standing portrait from belt height, a little ceiling, no collapse.

Fix: camera on the ground, looking straight up, verticals rushing inward. The other cousin is Ground Level along the street: you see a row of boots and a horizon.

Worm's-eye has almost no horizon; it has a zenith.

Questions

What is worm's-eye view in film?

A worm's-eye view looks sharply up from ground level or below the subject. Verticals collapse inward and the figure or building reads as a tower over the lens.

Worm's-eye view vs low angle

A low angle is a moderate look-up from below the eyes. Worm's-eye is extreme: floor or pit, looking straight up, almost no standing horizon, scale as threat or wonder.

When should I use worm's-eye view?

Use it when the subject should be a tower and the audience should be dust. Do not use it for ordinary dialogue power; use a low angle there.

How do I prompt worm's-eye view for AI image or video?

Write: Worm's-eye view from ground level looking straight up at [Subject], extreme low, verticals collapsing inward. Specify lens on the floor or in a pit, not waist height.

entries.title: Overhead Top-Down
entries.text:
Overhead Top-Down

Bird’s-eye tableauPlan zénithal

An overhead top-down shot looks nearly straight down at 90 degrees, flattening bodies and spaces into a graphic arrangement. Faces are scarce; silhouette, props, and the plan of the table or room do the talking.

Volume

Create this Overhead Top-Down

Narrative function

This is the crime scene, the place setting, the dance formation, the town drawn as a floor plan. People become pieces in a system.

Shadows draw on the surface because the camera is the ceiling. It can make an ordinary ritual strange by removing the social face.

A steep High Angle still has walls in perspective. A Bird's-Eye View still has altitude and drop.

Overhead wants the tabletop's geometry to match a plan: rectangles stay rectangles. If you still need the eyes, you are in the wrong viewpoint.

How it works

Mount the camera on an overhead rig, a high grid, or a virtual parent looking down the world Z-axis. Pitch at 90 degrees, roll chosen so the set's long axis sits square.

Arrange performers for silhouette: heads, hands, plates, chalk outlines. Because faces are less available, costume color and contrast have to carry identity.

Prompt: overhead top-down at 90 degrees, flat-lay or room plan, shadows as drawing.

When to use it

Use it for a table, a crime scene, or a dance formation that should read as a diagram. Concrete beat: four pairs of hands setting a long table, plates passing, the rectangle of the wood filling the frame.

Do not use it when the line is on a face.

Compared with similar shots

Bird's-Eye View is a steep look from a great height; overhead is the 90-degree plan, often closer. High Angle is oblique and keeps a readable face.

Crane Over is the move that can finish as this viewpoint. A product flat-lay is the still-life cousin; film overhead usually still includes a body as a piece in the plan.

Bird's-Eye ViewTurn life into a board game or a ritual.

Crane OverTurn a scene into a map without cutting.

Eye LevelDefault honesty. Do not look down or up unless you mean it.

In film

Dogville exposes the town as a floor-plan layout from above. The Grand Budapest Hotel uses top-down desks, pastries, and objects as graphic systems.

Oldboy's corridor coverage from above turns bodies into a moving diagram. Borrow the plan view, not the wallpaper.

Dogville 2003Overhead views expose the town’s floor-plan-like layout.

The Grand Budapest Hotel 2014Top-down object and desk compositions.

Prompt it

Lock 90 degrees and the rectangle. Quote: Overhead top-down shot of [Subject] at 90 degrees, flat-lay or room plan, shadows as drawing.

Add: camera straight down, tabletop or floor as a true rectangle, tops of heads, no three-quarter face. If the model tilts, say no perspective wedge on the table.

Use in Video Generator

Strict top-down locked shot of four people setting a long table, their hands passing plates in a coordinated pattern. The tabletop forms a clean rectangle, no perspective tilt, no camera rotation. One person stops and the system loses its rhythm.

What usually goes wrong

The usual wrong cousin is a steep High Angle that still shows a wall and a face. Tell: trapezoid table, eyeline into camera, room in perspective.

Fix: 90 degrees, plan geometry, silhouette clarity. The other failure is a bird's-eye city when you asked for a kitchen table: wrong scale.

Name the surface (table, bed, street as plan) and the distance.

Questions

What is overhead top-down in film?

An overhead shot looks nearly straight down at 90 degrees. Bodies and rooms flatten into a graphic plan; faces give way to silhouette and arrangement.

Overhead vs bird's-eye view

Overhead is a straight-down plan, often over a table, a body, or a marked floor. Bird's-eye view is from a great height, a map of a place with a sense of drop.

When should I use overhead top-down?

Use it when systems, evidence, or choreography should be legible as a diagram. Do not use it for a talking face.

How do I prompt overhead for AI image or video?

Write: Overhead top-down shot of [Subject] at 90 degrees, flat-lay or room plan, table or floor as a rectangle, shadows as drawing. Forbid an oblique high angle.

entries.title: Ground Level
entries.text:
Ground Level

A ground-level shot puts the lens almost on the floor, so boots, hems, wheels, and the dirt become actors. Height is the fact: the camera starts from the ground plane, whether it looks along the street or steeply up.

Create this Ground Level

Narrative function

From the dirt, a walk is a sequence of soles. A coat trailing, a wheel, a dropped gun, a snake's view of a street: the floor is the foreground and architecture goes large above it.

Westerns and car films live here because the ground is where decisions land. Worm's-Eye View is the cousin that looks straight up until there is no street, only a zenith.

Low Angle can be shot from the waist and never touch the floor. Hip Level still belongs to hands and holsters.

Ground-level is the pedestal on the boards.

How it works

Set the camera on a low plate, a sandbag, or a hole so the sensor is centimeters from the ground. A wide lens exaggerates the near boots and the far horizon.

You may look along the floor (track, tire, hem) or tilt up (a coat filling the sky). Keep grit, wet, or dust in the near field; that is how the height reads.

Prompt: ground-level camera, lens nearly on the floor, boots and trailing coat, horizon very low.

When to use it

Use it when the story starts from the dirt: an arrival on foot, a car, a body on the road. Concrete beat: boots stepping onto a dusty street, coat hem in the near field, town rising beyond.

Do not use it as the default for a walking conversation; that is Shoulder Level or Eye Level.

Compared with similar shots

Worm's-Eye View looks sharply up from this height until verticals collapse and the horizon dies. Low Angle is a pitch from below the eyes, not a requirement that the lens kiss the floor.

Hip Level sits at belt height so hands stay in the plane of focus. Overhead Top-Down is the opposite pole: the floor as a plan, not as a foreground.

Worm's-Eye ViewThe subject is a tower. You are dust.

Low AnglePower, monument, or intimidation.

Eye LevelDefault honesty. Do not look down or up unless you mean it.

In film

Once Upon a Time in the West lets the station boards, tracks, and boots own the opening; the ground is duration. Drive keeps cars, asphalt, and shoes in the near field so the street is the world.

Borrow the low pedestal and the near-ground texture.

Prompt it

Name the floor as foreground. Quote: Ground-level camera looking steeply up at [Subject], lens nearly on the floor, boots and trailing coat monumental.

If you want the along-the-dirt variant, say looking along the ground, boots in the near field, horizon low, not straight up at the sky.

Use in Image Generator

Ground-level camera looking steeply up at [Subject], lens nearly on the floor, boots and trailing coat monumental.

What usually goes wrong

The usual wrong cousin is Low Angle from kneeling height with a clean floor and a full face. Tell: no near-ground texture, no boots, camera clearly at knee-plus.

Fix: lens nearly on the floor, grit or pavement sharp in the foreground. If the shot is only nostrils and sky, you drifted into Worm's-Eye View.

Questions

What is ground level in film?

A ground-level shot places the lens almost on the floor. Boots, hems, wheels, and pavement become the near subject; the world rises from the dirt.

Ground level vs worm's-eye view

Ground level is a height: camera on the floor, often looking along boots or steeply up a coat. Worm's-eye view is an extreme upward pitch from that height, verticals collapsing, almost no street horizon.

When should I use ground level?

Use it when the ground is part of the beat: a walk, a car, a dropped object, a Western arrival. Do not use it for ordinary seated talk.

How do I prompt ground level for AI image or video?

entries.title: Dutch Angle
entries.text:
Dutch Angle

canted angleoblique angleDutch tiltCanted framingPlan débullé

A Dutch angle rolls the camera so verticals and the horizon appear tilted. The cant is usually static: gravity's down is no longer the bottom of the frame, which is why the world reads as off its axis.

Volume

Create this Dutch Angle

Narrative function

Pitch looks up or down. Roll breaks the floor.

A Dutch (canted, oblique) shot is a choice about gravity, not about power height. Use it when the moral or mental line is already bent: a sick city, a fight that will not stay fair, a mind that cannot stand up.

Adjacent level shots make the cant mean something. If every setup is Dutch, nothing is.

It is not a Low Angle. Looking up with a level roll is a different axis.

It is not a Dutch Roll either: that is the move that rotates into a cant during the shot. A static Dutch is a frozen decision.

How it works

Rotate the camera around the lens axis. A readable working cant is about 15 to 30 degrees; past 45 the frame often just looks like a mistake.

Compose diagonals on purpose: stair rails, streets, a leaning body that agrees or argues with the roll. Keep the set rigid.

The sensation should come from the viewpoint, not from warped walls. Decide whether the reverse stays level for contrast.

Prompt: Dutch angle, camera rolled 20 to 30 degrees, diagonal horizon.

When to use it

Use it when the world is off its axis. Concrete beat: a stairwell confrontation, banister as a diagonal, both feet still planted on real steps.

Do not use it as decoration on every villain or every night street.

Compared with similar shots

Eye Level with a level horizon is the control condition. Incline is a gentler cant, a few degrees of slope rather than a full lean.

Dutch Roll and Camera Roll are motion on this axis. Low Angle pitches up; High Angle pitches down.

Neither is a Dutch until you also roll.

Dutch RollUnease that arrives in time, not as a still cant.

Eye LevelDefault honesty. Do not look down or up unless you mean it.

High AngleVulnerability, surveillance, or a map of a room.

In film

The Third Man cants Vienna's streets and encounters so the postwar city will not sit true. Do the Right Thing angles selected confrontations rather than the whole film.

Mission: Impossible uses canted Prague coverage; the later rotating vault is a different trick (the set moves). Borrow a motivated static roll, not a permanent lean.

The Third Man 1949Canted views of Vienna’s streets and encounters.

Do the Right Thing 1989Angled compositions intensify selected confrontations.

Prompt it

Name the roll in degrees and keep the buildings straight. Quote: Dutch angle of [Subject], camera rolled 20 to 30 degrees, diagonal horizon, moral or mental tilt.

Add: static cant, walls rigid, not a low angle, not a rolling camera. If the model warps anatomy, say natural body proportions, only the horizon is tilted.

Use in Video Generator

A tenant confronts a landlord in a narrow stairwell. Static camera canted fifteen degrees, strong diagonal banister, rigid walls and natural anatomy. Both actors remain grounded. No rolling camera, fisheye distortion or vibrating image; the tension comes from the tilted composition.

What usually goes wrong

The usual wrong cousin is Low Angle (pitch) or a moving Dutch Roll. Tell: ceiling in frame but horizon level, or the camera rotating during the shot when you wanted a still lean.

Fix: level pitch, roll 20 to 30 degrees, lock it. The other failure is 60-degree decoration on every setup.

If the next shot is also canted, the cant has no contrast.

Questions

What is a Dutch angle in film?

A Dutch angle rolls the camera so the horizon and verticals tilt. The frame's relationship to gravity is broken on purpose, usually as a static cant.

Dutch angle vs low angle

A low angle pitches the camera up from below the eyes. A Dutch angle rolls the camera; the floor slants. You can combine them, but they are different axes.

When should I use a Dutch angle?

Use it when disequilibrium, aggression, or a stylized sick world should be in the geometry. Do not use it as a default mood for night or villains.

How do I prompt a Dutch angle for AI image or video?

Write: Dutch angle of [Subject], camera rolled 20 to 30 degrees, diagonal horizon, static cant, walls not warped. Say it is not a low angle and not a rolling camera.

entries.title: Point of View
entries.text:
Point of View

subjective cameraMuffled perspectiveTinnitus effect

A POV shot makes the camera function as a character's optical viewpoint: what they see at their eye height. The looker's head and shoulder stay out of the frame; we inhabit the look, not a seat behind it.

Volume

Create this Point of View

Narrative function

Classical coverage builds a POV as a sentence: a person looks, we cut to the seen, we often cut back to a reaction. Rear Window lives on that grammar.

The camera sits at their eyes, aims where they aim, and refuses the back of their head. Identification is forced because the audience is briefly the character.

It is not Over-the-Shoulder Coverage, which keeps the looker's shoulder as a claim of with, not as. It is not First-Person, which lets a body own the lens for a long ride: hands, breath, locomotion.

A POV can be a single still insert. First-person is a body that keeps seeing.

Subjective sound (a ringing ear, a mute beach) can ride with a POV or sit on an objective picture. Do not confuse a hearing filter with this optical setup.

How it works

Put the camera at the named character's eye height and point it along their eyeline. Match lens choice to their attention: a longer glass for binocular looking, a wider field for a panicked scan.

No owner body in frame unless a diegetic visor or mask is the optical device (Halloween). If you include a shoulder, you have left POV for OTS.

Prompt: what [Subject] sees, world at their eye height, no back of a head, no shoulder of the looker.

When to use it

Use it to force identification: the audience is the character for the length of the look. Concrete beat: a look offscreen, then empty tracks, steam, and lamps at their eye height.

Do not use it when you still need the looker's face in the same shot; shoot the look, then the POV, or use OTS.

Compared with similar shots

Over-the-Shoulder Coverage shows the near shoulder and the far face; we stand with the looker. First-Person adds hands, breath, and a body that owns the lens over time.

Object POV is a tool or vehicle seeing, not a person. Fourth Wall is the opposite look: eyes into our lens.

SnorriCam straps the camera to the body and looks at their face.

SnorriCamTrap the audience in a body that cannot get out.

Eye LevelDefault honesty. Do not look down or up unless you mean it.

High AngleVulnerability, surveillance, or a map of a room.

In film

Rear Window cuts from Jeff to binocular-aligned views of the courtyard. Halloween's opening adopts the observer's optical viewpoint through the mask.

Gravity moves into helmet-level seeing. Saving Private Ryan pairs optical shock with Miller's muted hearing; the sound is a cousin, not the definition of the shot.

Saving Private Ryan 1998Miller’s perception becomes muted during the Omaha Beach assault.

Sound of Metal 2019The soundtrack repeatedly shifts into Ruben’s changing hearing experience.

Gravity 2013Continuous-looking passages move between the astronaut, surrounding space and helmet-level subjectivity.

Halloween 1978The opening adopts the killer’s optical viewpoint before revealing the observer.

Lady in the Lake 1947Extended first-person detective storytelling.

Rear Window 1954Binocular and telephoto-looking views align with Jeff’s observation.

Prompt it

Describe the seen world, not the seer. Quote: What [Subject] sees: the world at their eye height, no back of a head, no shoulder of the looker in frame.

Name whose eyes, the height, and the object of the look. For video, one motivated pan or walk as that person, still without their shoulder.

Use in Video Generator

At a crowded celebration, a character becomes overwhelmed. Keep the image continuous while voices lose clarity, room detail recedes and a small nearby glass movement becomes unusually prominent. Return gradually to the room when a friend touches her shoulder. Build the perceptual transition in sound post-production.

What usually goes wrong

The usual wrong cousin is Over-the-Shoulder Coverage or a face looking toward camera. Tell: a blurry shoulder, the back of a head, or the looker staring at us.

Fix: empty of the owner, eyeline into the scene, height matched to the character you just showed looking. If hands and a gun enter and stay, you drifted into First-Person.

Questions

What is a POV shot in film?

A POV shot shows what a character sees from their eye height. The camera stands in for their eyes; the looker's head and shoulder are not in frame.

POV vs over-the-shoulder

POV is as the character: no owner body, only the seen world. Over-the-shoulder keeps a near shoulder in the foreground and the far face sharp; we are with them, not inside the look.

When should I use a POV shot?

Use it after a look, when identification with what they see is the beat: a courtyard, a threat, a visor. Do not use it as the only coverage of a conversation.

How do I prompt a POV shot for AI image or video?

Write: What [Subject] sees at their eye height, no back of head, no looker shoulder, [object of the look] filling the frame. Name whose viewpoint.

entries.title: Profile
entries.text:
Profile

A profile shot places the camera at 90 degrees to the head so one ear, the jaw, and the nose read as architecture, with the look offscreen. It is a true side view, not a three-quarter face and not a stamped coin if the living head still breathes.

Create this Profile

Narrative function

Turn the skull until the far eye disappears. What remains is silhouette, secrecy, and a sightline that refuses us.

A statue, a cameo, a don who will not grant the lens his other eye: profile withholds. The nose becomes a line against the background; the mouth can hide.

It is the wrong tool for most talk. Both eyes are how we read a lie.

If the beat needs charm, pain, or a clear listen, use Three-Quarter Angle. If they look into the lens, you wanted Fourth Wall, not a side.

How it works

Orbit until the camera sits on a line perpendicular to the subject's median plane. Keep height at Eye Level unless you are adding rank on purpose.

Light can graze the profile so the nose and brow separate from the field, or it can swallow the face into silhouette. Leave look-space in the direction of the nose.

Prompt: true profile, camera at 90 degrees to the head, one ear, nose as architecture, looking offscreen.

When to use it

Use it for statue, secrecy, or a nose as architecture. Concrete beat: a seated power figure in side view, looking toward an offscreen petitioner, one ear and a cigar.

Do not use it as default coverage of a two-person argument; you will lose the eyes.

Compared with similar shots

Three-Quarter Angle turns the face about 45 degrees so both eyes stay visible and the cheek recedes. Eye Level is a height, not a facing; a profile is often eye-level and 90 degrees yaw.

Point of View is the view they see, not the side of their head. Fourth Wall aims the eyes at us, the opposite of an offscreen profile look.

Three-Quarter AngleMost flattering narrative portrait.

Eye LevelDefault honesty. Do not look down or up unless you mean it.

High AngleVulnerability, surveillance, or a map of a room.

In film

Barry Lyndon uses painterly side views so court faces sit like plates without becoming cartoons. The Godfather often parks Vito in profile at the desk, looking toward petitioners rather than toward us.

Borrow the 90-degree head, the offscreen look, and a human face, not a cut-out.

Prompt it

Lock the yaw. Quote: True profile of [Subject], camera at 90 degrees to the head, one ear, the nose as architecture, looking offscreen.

A human face, not a stamped portrait. Add: far eye hidden, horizon level unless you intend a cant, look-space in front of the nose.

Use in Image Generator

True profile of [Subject], camera at 90 degrees to the head, one ear, the nose as architecture, looking offscreen. A human face, not a stamped portrait.

What usually goes wrong

The usual wrong cousin is Three-Quarter Angle: both eyes sneak back in. Tell: far iris visible, cheek still facing us.

Fix: rotate until the far eye is gone and the nose breaks the cheek line. The other failure is a paper cut-out with no skull volume.

Ask for a living head, skin, and one ear.

Questions

What is a profile shot in film?

A profile places the camera at 90 degrees to the head. You get one ear, the nose in side view, and a look offscreen; the far eye is hidden.

Profile vs three-quarter angle

Profile is a true side: one ear, far eye gone. Three-quarter turns the face about 45 degrees so both eyes remain and the far cheek recedes.

When should I use a profile shot?

Use it for concealment, formality, or a sightline that belongs offscreen. Do not use it when you need both eyes to carry a line.

How do I prompt a profile for AI image or video?

Write: True profile of [Subject], camera at 90 degrees to the head, one ear, nose as architecture, looking offscreen, far eye hidden. Say a human face, not a stamped portrait.

entries.title: Three-Quarter Angle
entries.text:
Three-Quarter Angle

A three-quarter angle turns the face about 45 degrees to the camera so both eyes remain visible and the far cheek recedes. It is the standard narrative portrait angle: dimensionality without a full front or a true side.

Create this Three-Quarter Angle

Narrative function

Most coverage of a talking face lives here. You see both eyes, the bridge of the nose, and a cheek going away, which is enough skull to light and enough access to read a listen.

It is useful because it models the head and still connects to an offscreen partner along a natural eyeline. It is the wrong tool when you want a coin (use Profile) or a confession into the taking lens (use Fourth Wall).

It is also not a height: you can shoot three-quarter from Eye Level, Low Angle, or High Angle. The name is yaw, not tilt.

How it works

Place the camera about 30 to 50 degrees off the subject's nose. Keep both irises; hide only a sliver of the far ear if any.

A 50mm to 85mm holds the head without stretching the near eye. Key from the far or near side depending on short or broad lighting; the angle is what gives the planes.

Prompt: three-quarter angle, face turned about 45 degrees, both eyes, classic portrait dimensionality.

When to use it

Use it as the default narrative portrait when a face must have volume and still belong to a scene. Concrete beat: a diner single, body open 45 degrees, eyeline to the partner off left, both eyes sharp.

Do not use it when concealment is the point; rotate to Profile.

Compared with similar shots

Profile is 90 degrees, one ear, far eye gone. Eye Level is how high the camera sits; three-quarter is how the head is turned.

Over-the-Shoulder Coverage often holds a three-quarter far face with a near shoulder chewing the frame. A full-front look into lens is Fourth Wall or an Interview eyeline, not three-quarter.

ProfileStatue, secrecy, or a nose as architecture.

Eye LevelDefault honesty. Do not look down or up unless you mean it.

High AngleVulnerability, surveillance, or a map of a room.

In film

Heat's diner encounter parks two faces in three-quarter so each man remains a full head while screen direction stays clean. Classical portrait coverage from studio-era close-ups through drawing-room films uses the same 45-degree turn to model a cheek.

Borrow the yaw and the two eyes, not a copied booth.

Prompt it

Name the turn in degrees and keep both eyes. Quote: Three-quarter angle on [Subject], face turned about 45 degrees, classic portrait dimensionality.

Add: both eyes visible, far cheek receding, not a true profile, not looking into the lens. Specify height separately (eye-level three-quarter, and so on).

Use in Image Generator

Three-quarter angle on [Subject], face turned about 45 degrees, classic portrait dimensionality.

What usually goes wrong

The usual wrong cousin is Profile (too much turn) or a passport front (too little). Tell: far eye gone, or both ears equally seen.

Fix: about 45 degrees, both irises, one ear dominant. The other failure is calling a Low Angle a three-quarter.

Pitch is not yaw; say both.

Questions

What is a three-quarter angle in film?

A three-quarter angle turns the face about 45 degrees to camera. Both eyes stay visible and the far cheek recedes, which is the default narrative portrait.

Three-quarter angle vs profile

Three-quarter keeps both eyes and a receding cheek. Profile is a 90-degree side view: one ear, nose as a line, far eye hidden.

When should I use a three-quarter angle?

Use it for most talking portraits that still need a connection to an offscreen partner. Use profile to withhold, or a look into lens to admit the audience.

How do I prompt a three-quarter angle for AI image or video?

Write: Three-quarter angle on [Subject], face turned about 45 degrees, both eyes visible, far cheek receding. Name camera height separately. Not profile, not into the lens.

entries.title: Reverse Angle
entries.text:
Reverse Angle

Delayed object of the lookRestricted coverage

A reverse-angle shot views the same spatial relationship from the opposing side, completing the axis of a look, a dialogue, or a standoff. Geography flips; the 180-degree line is respected so screen direction still matches.

Volume

Create this Reverse Angle

Narrative function

Someone looks. The reverse is who or what occupies the other pole.

In a diner, it is the other booth. In a gunfight, it is the other holster.

Matching size and height keeps the cut from feeling like a new scene. The reverse can be a clean Single or an Over-the-Shoulder Coverage; the name is the axis, not the foreground shoulder.

Withholding the reverse is a different editorial choice: a look, a reaction, and no answering view. The Blair Witch Project and Rosemary's Baby live on that denial.

The reverse-angle shot itself is the answering camera, not the refusal of it.

How it works

Hold the 180-line. Move the camera to the opposite side of the axis, still on the same side of the line, and match lens height to the new subject (sit versus stand, adult versus child).

Match shot size to the outgoing picture unless the cut is meant to punch. Eyelines must cross the same empty air.

Prompt: reverse angle, opposing view of the dialogue or standoff, 180-line respected, geography flipping.

When to use it

Use it to complete the axis: show who they were looking at. Concrete beat: after a look across a table, the matching-size single of the other person, eyeline opposing.

Do not fire the reverse when the scene's power is the withheld object of the look.

Compared with similar shots

Over-the-Shoulder Coverage is a composition often used as the reverse, with a near shoulder; a reverse can also be a clean Single. Point of View shows what they see, which may not be a face.

Eye Level may match on both sides, but the reverse is the opposing camera, not a height. Profile two-shots can reverse into opposing profiles.

Over-the-Shoulder CoverageDefault dialogue coverage with spatial glue.

Eye LevelDefault honesty. Do not look down or up unless you mean it.

High AngleVulnerability, surveillance, or a map of a room.

In film

Heat's diner keeps clear opposing screen directions on two three-quarter singles. The Good, the Bad and the Ugly builds the cemetery standoff from answering views along one axis.

The Shining's red-bathroom talk uses startling opposing spatial views. Neighbors (1920) is an early lesson in preserving orientation across reverses.

The Blair Witch Project 1999Characters’ reactions and restricted recorded views withhold much of the threat.

Rosemary’s Baby 1968Partial views and delayed information keep the spectator outside complete knowledge.

Heat 1995The diner encounter maintains clear opposing screen directions.

Neighbors 1920Editing preserves the action’s spatial orientation.

The Shining 1980The red-bathroom conversation with Grady uses startling opposing spatial views.

Tokyo Story 1953Conversation coverage follows a spatial system different from conventional Hollywood axis continuity.

Prompt it

Describe both poles even if you generate one still. Quote: Reverse angle on [Subject], the opposing view of a dialogue or standoff, 180-line respected, geography flipping.

Add: matching size to the first angle, opposing eyeline, same room, camera on the other side of the axis. For a pair, specify who was in the outgoing shot.

Use in Video Generator

Close-up of a caretaker opening a basement door just outside frame. Her expression changes as she sees something below, but hold on her face and the dark edge of the doorway. A quiet mechanical clicking comes from downstairs. Never cut to what she sees during this shot.

What usually goes wrong

The usual wrong cousin is a new setup that crosses the line or changes size for no reason. Tell: both faces look camera-right, or a wide answering a choker.

Fix: opposing eyelines, matched height and size, 180-line held. The other mix-up is Point of View: an empty doorway they were watching is a POV, not a reverse on the other person.

Questions

What is a reverse angle in film?

A reverse angle shows the same spatial relationship from the opposing side. It completes a look or a dialogue axis while keeping the 180-degree line.

Reverse angle vs over-the-shoulder

A reverse is the opposing camera on the axis. Over-the-shoulder is a framing that often serves as that reverse, with a near shoulder in the foreground. The reverse can also be a clean single.

When should I use a reverse angle?

Use it when the audience must see the other pole of a look, a talk, or a standoff. Do not use it when withholding the object of the look is the point.

How do I prompt a reverse angle for AI image or video?

Write: Reverse angle on [Subject], opposing view of the dialogue or standoff, 180-line respected, matching size, eyeline opposite the first shot. Name the geography that should flip.

entries.title: Trunk Shot
entries.text:
Trunk Shot

View from inside a container

A trunk shot places the camera inside a car trunk or similar confined pit, looking up at the people who open it, with the lid and rim framing their downward looks. It is a located low viewpoint, not a generic look-up in a parking lot.

Volume

Create this Trunk Shot

Narrative function

The audience is the object or the concealed body. Two faces appear over a bright lid; they look down at us; the dark rim eats the edges.

Power and curiosity swap: the standing people have the height, the camera has the secret. Tarantino's crime grammar made the car trunk a signature, but any container (a crate, an instrument case) can host the same physics.

A Low Angle on a street has no lid. A Worm's-Eye View on a tower has no one looking into the lens.

If you cannot see the opening, you do not have the shot.

How it works

Put a low camera in a trunk, a box, or an open-bottom set piece. Keep the container edge in frame on several sides.

Stage the lid's movement and aim the actors' eyelines at the same interior point. Daylight or a parking-lamp key from above is motivated by the open lid; the interior stays in shadow.

Prompt: trunk shot looking up from inside a car trunk or confined pit, rim framing the faces.

When to use it

Use it when someone is in the trunk, or when the reveal should come from inside a container. Concrete beat: two people pop a lid and lean in, looking down at the lens, dark rim against a bright sky.

Do not use it as a decorative low-angle on standing gangsters with no car.

Compared with similar shots

Low Angle looks up without a container. Worm's-Eye View looks up at architecture from the dirt.

Object POV can live inside a thing, but usually as the thing moving through the world, not as people opening it. Point of View of a bound captive can coincide with a trunk shot when the occupant is a character we have already met.

Low AnglePower, monument, or intimidation.

Worm's-Eye ViewThe subject is a tower. You are dust.

Eye LevelDefault honesty. Do not look down or up unless you mean it.

In film

Pulp Fiction views Jules and Vincent from inside the car trunk as they look down. Reservoir Dogs stages the same downward look into an open trunk.

Kill Bill and From Dusk Till Dawn reuse the pit-and-lid grammar. Borrow the rim, the lid, and the eyelines into the box.

Reservoir Dogs 1992Characters are seen looking down into the open trunk.

Pulp Fiction 1994Jules and Vincent are viewed from inside the car trunk.

Prompt it

The rim is mandatory. Quote: Trunk shot looking up at [Subject] from inside a car trunk or similar confined pit, playful low-angle signature.

Add: dark container edge framing the frame, lid or sky above, actors looking down into the lens, camera not rising out of the box.

Use in Video Generator

From inside an old wooden instrument case, look upward as two conservators open the lid and lean over it. The dark case rim frames their faces against a bright workshop ceiling. Clear lid movement, coherent downward eyelines, no camera rise or reveal of the observer.

What usually goes wrong

The usual wrong cousin is a generic Low Angle in a driveway. Tell: full standing bodies, no lid, no rim, horizon of a parking lot.

Fix: inside the trunk, rim in frame, faces leaning over an opening, downward eyelines. If the camera floats up and reveals the observer, you left the container.

Questions

What is a trunk shot in film?

A trunk shot looks up from inside a car trunk or similar pit. The lid and rim frame people looking down, so the camera sits where an object or captive would sit.

Trunk shot vs low angle

A low angle looks up from below eye level anywhere. A trunk shot is specifically inside a container; without the opening and the rim, it is just a low angle.

When should I use a trunk shot?

Use it when the viewpoint belongs in a trunk, a crate, or a case, and the standing people are looking in. Do not use it as a style sticker on any crime scene.

How do I prompt a trunk shot for AI image or video?

Write: Trunk shot looking up at [Subject] from inside a car trunk, dark rim framing the faces, lid open, actors looking down into the lens. Say the camera stays in the pit.

entries.title: Hip Level
entries.text:
Hip Level

A hip-level shot sits the camera around belt or holster height so hands, gait, and weapons share the plane of focus. It is a height choice, usually with a level horizon: the hands will decide.

Volume

Create this Hip Level

Narrative function

Westerns minted it because a draw happens at the belt. The face is still in the upper frame, but the story is in the fingers, the buckle, the coat hem at the wrist.

Tension reads before anyone looks up. Crime films stole the height for a gun that might come out during a talk.

It is not a Cowboy Shot, which is a frame size from mid-thigh up and can be taken from eye height. It is not a Low Angle unless you also pitch up.

Hip-level can stay level and still make the holster the equator of the picture.

How it works

Pedestal to belt height on a standing adult (roughly 90 to 110 cm). Keep roll level.

A slight look-up is optional; a true hip-level often aims through the hands toward the far figure. Depth of field should hold the holster and the facing body.

A wider lens at this height will stretch legs; a longer lens compresses the standoff. Prompt: hip-level camera, gunbelt height, hands and holster in the plane of focus.

When to use it

Use it when the hands will decide: a standoff, a pocketed weapon, a key passed at waist height. Concrete beat: two standing figures, belts in a line, fingers idle near leather.

Do not use it when the face is the only event; rise to Shoulder Level or Eye Level.

Compared with similar shots

Cowboy Shot crops mid-thigh as a size; hip-level is where the lens sits. Ground Level is on the dirt and privileges boots.

Low Angle pitches up for monument. Shoulder Level is a walking companion, closer to the face.

Eye Level ignores the belt.

Cowboy ShotShow hands, weapons, or stance without going full body.

Ground LevelStart from the dirt.

Eye LevelDefault honesty. Do not look down or up unless you mean it.

In film

The Good, the Bad and the Ugly keeps holsters and hands alive in the line of the lens during standoffs. No Country for Old Men works at belt and pocket height so a captured bolt pistol is as present as a face.

Borrow the height of the hands, not a copied desert.

Prompt it

Name belt height, not low camera. Quote: Hip-level camera on [Subject], gunbelt height, Western stance, hands and holster in the plane of focus.

Add: horizon through the hands, level roll, face still in the upper frame, not a worm's-eye, not mid-thigh crop unless you also want a cowboy size.

Use in Image Generator

What usually goes wrong

The usual wrong cousin is a Low Angle power tilt or a Cowboy Shot from standing eye height. Tell: nostrils and ceiling, or a mid-thigh crop taken from above the chest.

Fix: camera at belt, looking through the hands, horizon level. If only boots are sharp, you dropped to Ground Level.

Questions

What is hip level in film?

A hip-level shot places the camera at belt or holster height. Hands, gait, and weapons sit in the plane of focus; the face remains in the upper frame.

Hip level vs cowboy shot

Hip level is camera height at the belt. A cowboy shot is a frame size from mid-thigh up. You can combine them, but a cowboy can also be taken from eye height.

When should I use hip level?

Use it when hands and a possible draw are the beat. Do not use it for a seated talk or a face that needs to fill the frame.

entries.title: Shoulder Level
entries.text:
Shoulder Level

A shoulder-level camera sits slightly below the eyes, at the height of a walking companion. It is less formal than true Eye Level and less monumental than a Low Angle; the face is still the target, seen from the deltoid rather than the pupil.

Create this Shoulder Level

Narrative function

You stay with a mover without dropping into chaotic Handheld grammar. The lens is where another body would be: beside them on a street, a few inches low, able to take a bump.

Hurt Locker bomb walks and Goodfellas nightclub approaches often live in this band because the camera can travel as a person would. It is not Over-the-Shoulder Coverage.

OTS is a foreground shoulder of a different body. Shoulder-level can be a clean Single or a Follow Shot with no near shoulder at all.

The name is pedestal height.

How it works

Set the camera at clavicle or deltoid height, typically 5 to 20 cm below the subject's eyes. Keep the horizon close to level; a tiny look-up is natural from this height and should not grow into a power tilt.

A 35mm is a common walking companion. Stabilization (Steadicam, Gimbal Shot) keeps the height without adding shake as style.

Prompt: shoulder-level camera, slightly below the eyes, walking companion's view.

When to use it

Use it to stay with a mover as a companion, especially through rooms and streets. Concrete beat: walking a few feet off a soldier or a host, lens at their shoulder, face readable, floor not dominating.

Do not use it as a substitute for messy handheld, and do not call an OTS this unless the only fact you mean is height.

Compared with similar shots

Eye Level matches the pupils and reads as equal portrait. Hip Level drops to the belt.

Low Angle pitches up on purpose. Over-the-Shoulder Coverage includes a near person's shoulder; shoulder-level need not.

Point of View removes the companion and becomes the mover's eyes. Follow Shot is the path; shoulder-level is the height of that path.

Eye LevelDefault honesty. Do not look down or up unless you mean it.

High AngleVulnerability, surveillance, or a map of a room.

Low AnglePower, monument, or intimidation.

In film

The Hurt Locker often stays at soldier height through streets and rooms so the walk is shared, not observed from a balcony. Goodfellas' Copacabana approach rides at companion height through the kitchen: we arrive with Henry, not as his eyes and not as a crane.

Borrow the pedestal, not the whole tracking route.

Prompt it

Separate height from move. Quote: Shoulder-level camera on [Subject], slightly below the eyes, a walking companion's view, less formal than true eye-level.

Add: horizon nearly level, not a low-angle, no foreground shoulder unless you also want OTS. For video, one follow at that height, no tour.

Use in Image Generator

Shoulder-level camera on [Subject], slightly below the eyes, a walking companion's view, less formal than true eye-level.

What usually goes wrong

The usual wrong cousin is true Eye Level (too high and formal) or a Low Angle (too much pitch). Tell: matched pupils, or a ceiling grab.

Fix: camera at the shoulder, slight look-up at most, companion distance. If a blurry shoulder of another actor eats the frame, you wrote OTS.

If hands of the subject enter as if we were them, you wrote First-Person.

Questions

What is shoulder level in film?

Shoulder-level places the camera slightly below the subject's eyes, at walking-companion height. It is a pedestal choice, usually with a nearly level horizon.

Shoulder level vs eye level

Eye level matches the pupils and reads as equal, formal coverage. Shoulder level sits a few inches lower, like a person walking beside them, less of a portrait lock.

When should I use shoulder level?

Use it to stay with a mover without a power tilt or a formal eye lock. Do not use it when you need peer-to-peer stillness or a holster-plane standoff.

How do I prompt shoulder level for AI image or video?

Write: Shoulder-level camera on [Subject], slightly below the eyes, walking companion's view, horizon nearly level. Say not eye-level and not a low-angle. For motion, follow at that height.

entries.title: First-Person
entries.text:
First-Person

FPV charactersubjective camera

A first-person camera makes the lens function as a character's bodily viewpoint, with a body that owns it: hands entering the frame, breath, tools, locomotion. It is subjective seeing as continuous embodiment, not a single optical insert.

Volume

Create this First-Person

Narrative function

The audience is the character for a stretch of time. Lady in the Lake tries to tell a detective story this way.

Hardcore Henry runs it as an action body. Enter the Void keeps the camera inside a consciousness that still has a path through rooms.

Hands, a steering wheel, a gun, a door handled at the edge: those are the tells that a person, not an invisible observer, is looking. A Point of View shot can be one cut of what they see, clean of the owner.

First-person keeps the owner as a felt body. Object POV parents the camera to a prop instead.

SnorriCam looks at their face from their chest, which is the opposite ownership.

How it works

Parent the camera to the character's head or upper chest with a human field of view (roughly 24mm to 35mm spherical, not a tiny action-cam unless that is diegetic). Allow hands, shoulders at the extreme edge, or a tool to enter.

Add breath and footfall as camera motion only as much as a body would. Do not show the owner's face except in glass.

Prompt: first-person camera as [Subject] would see, hands entering frame, breath, a body that owns the lens.

When to use it

Use it when the audience must be the character, not merely glance as them. Concrete beat: running a wet overpass, gloved hands hitting the rail, breath in the cold, no face of the runner.

Do not use it for a two-shot argument; you will lose the listener.

Compared with similar shots

Point of View is the optical slice of the seen world, often an insert after a look, owner body forbidden. Object POV is a ball, a bullet, a phone, a vehicle.

Over-the-Shoulder Coverage keeps us behind someone we can still see. Fourth Wall has them look at us.

SnorriCam bolts the camera to the torso and stares at their face while the world slides.

Point of ViewForce identification. The audience is the character.

SnorriCamTrap the audience in a body that cannot get out.

Object POVThe prop has eyes.

In film

Hardcore Henry keeps the body in the lens: hands, weapons, impacts. Enter the Void rides a consciousness through space after the body is gone, still as a moving first-person path.

Lady in the Lake (1947) attempts extended first-person detective storytelling, other characters addressing the lens as Marlowe. Use those as embodiment grammar.

Prompt it

Require a body at the edges. Quote: First-person camera as [Subject] would see, hands entering frame, breath, a body that owns the lens.

Video: First-person view moving as [Subject] moves, hands or tools entering the edges. Add: no owner's face except a reflection, eye height of that person, not a drone, not an OTS shoulder.

Use in Video Generator

First-person view moving as [Subject] moves, hands or tools entering the edges.

What usually goes wrong

The usual wrong cousin is a clean Point of View plate (no hands) or a Follow Shot behind the actor. Tell: a back of a head, or a perfectly disembodied lock-off of a room.

Fix: hands or a tool in frame, motion as a walk or a turn of the head, owner invisible as a face. If the camera is bolted to a car hood with chrome in frame, you wanted Object POV.

Questions

What is first-person camera in film?

First-person makes the camera a character's body: we see as they see, with hands, breath, or tools entering the frame. It is continuous embodiment, not only a glance.

First-person vs POV

A POV shot is what they see, often a single insert with no owner body. First-person keeps a body owning the lens over time: hands, locomotion, breath.

When should I use first-person?

Use it when the audience should inhabit a body for a passage of action or perception. Do not use it for ordinary reverse-shot dialogue.

How do I prompt first-person for AI image or video?

Write: First-person camera as [Subject] would see, hands entering frame, breath, a body that owns the lens. For video, move as they move, tools at the edges, no owner's face.

entries.title: Fourth Wall
entries.text:
Fourth Wall

NarrationSubjective verbal commentary

A fourth-wall look aims the subject's eyes into the taking lens, so the scene admits an audience. The camera is no longer an invisible observer; it is a person in the room, or the spectator the character has decided to include.

Volume

Create this Fourth Wall

Narrative function

Theatre named the fourth wall; film breaks it when a Ferris explains the day to us, when a killer in Funny Games checks whether we are still complicit, when Alvy steps out of Annie Hall to argue. The eyeline is the mechanism.

Everything else in the shot can stay naturalistic. The turn is the look into glass.

It is not Point of View (we see what they see). It is not a diary voiceover laid over a face that never finds the lens (Taxi Driver's narration can run without a break).

It is close to Interview, except interview eyeline is usually just off-lens, to a listener, while fourth-wall treats us as the partner.

How it works

Place the camera at the subject's eye height and put their eyeline in the center of the taking lens (or a marked pupil on the matte box). Keep the rest of the blocking honest so the look is the only rupture.

A slight Eye Level three-quarter that then turns into the glass can stage the break as a decision. Prompt: fourth-wall look, eyes into the lens, the scene admitting an audience.

When to use it

Use it when they know we are here: a plan explained to us, a dare, a confession that includes the spectator. Concrete beat: a character pauses in a room, finds the lens, and continues the line to us.

Do not sprinkle random winks; the break has to change the contract of the scene.

Compared with similar shots

Point of View inhabits their look into the world. First-Person is their body seeing; other people may look at camera as if at that body, which is diegetic address, not a break.

Interview aims just off-lens to an offscreen questioner. Profile looks away.

Reverse Angle answers another character, not us.

Point of ViewForce identification. The audience is the character.

InterviewSomeone is answering a question we did not hear.

Eye LevelDefault honesty. Do not look down or up unless you mean it.

In film

Ferris Bueller's Day Off lets Ferris comment on his own behavior directly to viewers. Funny Games uses looks (and more) to implicate the spectator.

Annie Hall lets Alvy address the audience and step outside ordinary scene realism. The Office glances at the lens as documentary embarrassment, a softer cousin of the same eyeline.

Taxi Driver 1976Travis’s diary-like narration frames his view of the city.

Badlands 1973Holly’s narration creates distance from the events being shown.

Ferris Bueller’s Day Off 1986Ferris explains and comments on his behavior directly to viewers.

Annie Hall 1977Alvy addresses the audience and steps outside ordinary scene realism.

Funny Games 1997Direct looks and overt manipulation implicate the spectator.

Prompt it

The eyeline is the law. Quote: Fourth-wall look from [Subject], eyes into the lens, the scene admitting an audience.

Add: both eyes to camera, eye-level, not a profile, not looking just off-lens as in an interview. If they were in a scene with others, say the others do not look at camera unless that is the joke.

Use in Video Generator

A meticulous traveler narrates how carefully she plans every journey while the images show her repeatedly improvising: borrowing a map, following a stranger’s gesture and boarding at the last moment. Write restrained original narration that reveals self-image through contradiction rather than explaining visible actions.

What usually goes wrong

The usual wrong cousin is Interview (eyeline off-lens) or a Point of View of another character (someone looking at the first-person body). Tell: they look past the camera, or we see what they see instead of their eyes.

Fix: pupils on the lens, address to the audience. Voiceover without a look is narration, not this shot.

Questions

What is fourth wall in film?

Breaking the fourth wall means a character looks into the taking lens and admits the audience. The eyeline into the camera is the break.

Fourth wall vs POV

Fourth wall looks at us. A POV shot is what the character sees in their world. One admits a spectator; the other inhabits a looker.

When should I use fourth wall?

Use it when the contract of the scene should include the audience: explanation, dare, complicity. Do not use it as a random wink with no change in address.

How do I prompt fourth wall for AI image or video?

Write: Fourth-wall look from [Subject], eyes into the lens, eye-level, the scene admitting an audience. Not an interview off-lens look, not a POV of the scenery.

entries.title: Object POV
entries.text:
Object POV

Vehicle-mounted perspectiveRigid object attachment

An object-POV shot is the viewpoint of a tool, a ball, a bullet, a phone, or a vehicle: the prop has eyes. The camera is parented to that object, so the object stays stable in the frame while the world moves relative to it.

Volume

Create this Object POV

Narrative function

Agency leaves the invisible observer and goes to a machine or a thing. A fork of a bicycle stays in the corner while cobbles rush.

A car body is fixed and the desert tears past. A phone slides across a table toward a face.

Sports broadcasts have lived here for decades (puck, stump, helmet). The motion is tactile because the mount cannot independently decide to drift.

It is not First-Person, which is a human body with hands and breath. It is not a free drone that happens to start near a prop.

If the anchor object wanders inside the frame, the parent is broken.

How it works

Use a professionally secured mount or a rigid virtual parent transform on the named object. Include a visible part of the anchor (barrel, rubber, chrome, glass edge).

Preserve vibration that belongs to the object; do not add a second operator path. Lens choice is often wide because the mount is close.

Prompt: object POV as if [Subject] were seen from a tool, a ball, a bullet, a phone: the thing looking.

When to use it

Use it when the prop has eyes: a weapon, a vehicle, a thrown thing, a camera that is diegetic. Concrete beat: viewpoint from a phone sliding toward a face, the phone's bezel fixed at the frame edge.

Do not use it as a pretty fly-around that ignores the object.

Compared with similar shots

First-Person is a human body owning the lens. Point of View is a character's optical insert, usually without a gadget rim.

Locked-On glues a subject in frame while the world streams; object-POV is looking from the object, often with the object as foreground. Trunk Shot is a pit people open, not a tool in flight.

FPV Drone is a flying body of its own.

First-PersonThe audience is the character.

Point of ViewForce identification. The audience is the character.

Eye LevelDefault honesty. Do not look down or up unless you mean it.

In film

Mad Max: Fury Road keeps parts of pursuing machines fixed while the desert tears past. Leviathan (2012) mounts cameras on fishing equipment and bodies at sea so the work, not an observer, sees.

Sports broadcasts use puck and vehicle mounts as the same grammar. Hardcore Henry inserts gadget viewpoints inside an otherwise human first-person film.

Mad Max: Fury Road 2015Vehicle-mounted views keep parts of the pursuing machines fixed while the desert tears past.

Leviathan 2012Cameras move with fishing equipment and bodies at sea.

Prompt it

Name the object and keep it fixed in frame. Quote: Object POV as if [Subject] were seen from a tool, a ball, a bullet, a phone: the thing looking.

Video: Viewpoint of an object moving toward or around [Subject]. Add: a visible piece of the anchor object locked in the foreground, rigid mount, world moving, no detached drone path.

Use in Video Generator

Camera rigidly attached beside the front fork of an old bicycle, looking ahead. The fork stays fixed in the lower-left frame while cobblestones rush beneath and street corners swing with the steering. Real wheel rotation and restrained mechanical vibration; no detached drone movement.

What usually goes wrong

The usual wrong cousin is First-Person (human hands) or a free-flying camera. Tell: breath and fingers, or the phone drifting around inside the shot.

Fix: parent the camera to the named prop, show the prop's edge, keep that edge locked. If people open a lid and look in, you wanted Trunk Shot.

Questions

What is object POV in film?

Object POV is the viewpoint of a prop or vehicle. The camera is attached to that thing, so the thing stays put in the frame while the world moves.

Object POV vs first-person

First-person is a human body: hands, breath, eye height of a person. Object POV is a tool, ball, bullet, phone, or machine looking, with the object as the mount.

When should I use object POV?

Use it when a prop should see: a vehicle chase from the machine, a thrown camera, a diegetic gadget. Do not use it for a person's glance; that is POV or first-person.

How do I prompt object POV for AI image or video?

Write: Object POV from [named prop], a piece of the object locked in the foreground, [Subject] seen from that mount, world moving around a rigid camera. For video, the object travels; the camera does not detach.
